The old agency pricing model is dying. Most founders are still trying to save it.

Average project budget in 2017: sixty thousand euros. 
In 2021: forty thousand euros.

And it has kept falling since.

Agencies running 2017's playbook are doing 2017's margins in a 2026 market. And that math does not work.

Then how are some of the agencies still crushing it?

Outcome-based pricing. Charge for pipeline, meetings, revenue delivered.

Retainers and hourly billing belong to 2017.

When AI does the work, outcomes are the only pricing where margins hold.

Most "AI for agencies" tools were never priced for agencies.

They were priced for SaaS sales teams, where seats expand as the org grows, volume tiers compound, and the product stays always-on against a predictable pipeline.

The math depends on a customer that has a sales team and keeps adding seats to it.

Agencies don't run on that math.

They have founders, a small biz dev function, and a delivery team that can't sit on outbound because they're billable on client work.

Revenue is project-based, utilization is tight, and outbound runs in spikes between deliveries.

Drop a tool priced for the SaaS world inside that shape and the ROI math collapses while the invoice keeps arriving.

there's a version of the @sortlist story that fits in a tweet. four of us started it in brussels in 2014, raised about €18m across three rounds, crossed 4,000 paying agencies on the platform, currently on our way to $10m arr, and i got handed the ceo seat last june.

that version is true and also useless.

here's the longer one with the unfiltered details.

in 2013 we were running a small digital marketing agency on the side of school. four of us, all at solvay business school in brussels: thibaut, charles, michael, and me. we were billing decent money for that age, and the work itself was fine, nothing remarkable.

the question that ended up mattering came from our clients.

every project ended the same way. somebody would say 'next quarter we need an agency for seo, or paid, or content, who should we hire?' we'd recommend someone, they'd come back happy, and we never made a cent on the recommendation.

at some point one of us said it out loud. the recommendation was the actual product, and the agency work was just how we kept getting asked the question.

so we built sortlist.

except for the first stretch sortlist was really just a consultancy that called itself a marketplace. four students in a dorm room, hand-registering the first wave of agencies into the platform ourselves and manually matching the companies that came in to the agencies that fit them. we were the algorithm.

this is the part most marketplace founders won't admit. marketplaces almost always start as services, and the platform layer comes later.

in february 2015, lean fund handed us €550k. that wasn't validation so much as permission to stop running the side agency and bet the whole thing on the marketplace.

then comes the part of the story that sounds the same in every founder bio. we raised a €2m series a in 2019, acquired a Spanish competitor and then a german one through 2020, and closed an €11m series b in 2021. by then we'd crossed 4,000 paying agencies on the platform, 600,000 buyers were searching for one every month, and customers like mastercard, revolut, renault and accor were on it.

i could stop writing here and the post would do well. it's a clean arc with tidy numbers from a dorm room to a series b, the kind of thing that gets pinned to a profile. but the next two years are the part i actually want to write about.

in 2022 and 2023, sortlist almost died.

the post-zirp world arrived faster than our growth targets could adjust, and we'd hired into a future that wasn't coming. so we cut headcount from 140 to 70 across those two years, roughly half the company. on a podcast earlier this year i admitted, publicly for the first time, that i'd considered leaving during that stretch. i didn't, but it wasn't a clean no.

survival is mostly a series of decisions you don't broadcast. we hit operational profitability in 2024, and the road there wasn't anything you'd want to teach.

on june 3rd 2025, thibaut, who'd led sortlist for eleven years as ceo, handed me the seat. nothing was broken and we hadn't fallen out. it was a collective decision about what the next chapter needs, which is a different operating posture than the last one did. that's the cleanest way i know to describe it. handoffs like this get read as pivots more often than they should. most of them are just operating-posture changes that the outside can't see.

six months later, in december 2025, we made the largest acquisition in our history when we bought overloop, a brussels-based outbound platform with customers across the world. we framed it publicly as an outbound move, although inside the company we'd already decided it was the start of our ai bet.

in january 2026 i told the team we were going all-in on ai. our non-engineers started shipping production code through an internal slack-to-claude bot, and an experiment with claude running as an sdr landed real customer meetings inside two weeks.

betting a 12-year-old company on ai is a different exercise than starting one fresh, and most of the playbooks being published this year are written by people doing the second.

twelve years from four students hand-registering agencies in a brussels dorm, we're betting the next chapter on the proposition that the next decade of agency-finding doesn't look like the last one. that's the actual stake. everything else is just funding rounds.

i'm on x because the conversations about what ai does to services businesses, about agencies, about outbound, about the things i've actually spent twelve years inside of, are happening on this platform now. they aren't on linkedin anymore.

if you're new, here's what i'm going to be writing about:

- the agency economy and what's actually happening to it. 
- signal-based outbound, before everyone calls it something else. 
- what it looks like to bet a 12-year-old company on ai instead of starting a new one. 
- the small operator decisions that compound, the ones that don't make it into the founder podcasts. 

and occasionally, when it's worth it, the part of the story i usually leave out.

that's me. welcome.

Every single intent signal worth watching in 2026:

JOB

1. Job postings. They opened a role you can map to a pain you solve. Send the hiring manager three lines, quoting the JD back at them. Don't pitch the product yet.

2. Reposted jobs. Same role, listed twice. The first attempt didn't close. Show up with the candidate-shaped alternative before they burn another quarter.

3. Hiring campaigns. Multiple roles inside a short window. A whole function is scaling. Pitch what makes the new team productive on day one. The tool sale comes later.

4. Job changes. Your champion moves, or a buyer you lost lands somewhere new. Reach out in week one with something useful. New hires get a 60-day budget window. Almost nobody hits it.

SOCIAL

1. Competitor tracking. They engage with a competitor's content or page. The highest-intent social signal you'll buy. Skip the us-vs-them copy. Lead with the second-order problem the competitor won't solve, the one their customer hits in month three.

2. Social mentions. A decision-maker writes about a topic in your space on LinkedIn. Comment in their thread before you DM. Send a useful resource before you send a pitch.

3. Post reactions. They liked or reposted industry content. The thinnest signal you'll work with, useless on its own and worth something only when stacked under heavier signals.

4. Influencer post reactions. Engagement on a thought leader's post. Read it as topic curiosity and nothing more.

5. Company post reactions. Someone reacted to your target company's page. Useful for warming an account already in your pipeline. Don't open a new account off it.

6. New followers. New follows on a competitor or partner page. Treat this as market-map intel. It tells you who is interested in the category weeks before they show up in a job posting or an RFP.

COMPANY

1. New companies. A company was just registered. No vendor relationships, nothing locked in. Be the first one in their inbox with a starter package. Save the enterprise pitch for later.

2. Tenders & RFPs. Procurement opens. The highest stated intent on the entire list. Budget approved, scope written, timeline locked. This is a response motion, not an outbound one, and without an RFP playbook the signal is wasted.

FUNDING

1. Fundraising. The company just raised. Budget opens in the quarter after the close, rarely on the day of it. Time your outreach to 30-60 days post-announce. Day one their inbox is a graveyard.

2. Mergers & Acquisitions. They bought or got bought. Stack consolidations and vendor reviews follow inside the first 90 days. Pitch the migration help, the integration, the thing that survives the post-deal cleanup.

Take things further by stacking the intent signals on top of each other, and get better response rates as a result.
Some examples:

> Reposted jobs + Fundraising on the same account is a scaling team with budget approved.
> Tenders & RFPs + M&A on the same account is a company rewriting procurement rules after a consolidation.

Note: Two signals together aren't additive, they multiply.

Intent data is the loudest and the most poorly used category in B2B sales right now.

Most teams track one signal type (job postings) and ignore the rest.

Four buckets actually matter when you run outbound:

Job, Social, Company, Funding.

Job postings sit at the entry of the first bucket. The other thirteen signals across the four rarely get touched.

Take Job signals for instance.

A first-time job posting and a reposted job are completely different triggers.

When a role gets reposted three weeks later, the hiring manager has already burned through the obvious candidate list, the budget conversation happened a month ago, and the urgency is real. We write that first message acknowledging the situation directly. The "congrats on the new role" filler gets ignored when the role isn't new.

The Funding bucket has its own rhythm.

A fresh round opens a window of roughly ninety days where the CEO signs checks she wouldn't sign twelve months later.

Past that window the budget is committed to the incumbent stack and you're queueing behind whoever moved faster. Simply put, the signal expires.

The Company bucket is where the most expensive signal lives: tenders and RFPs. They cost more to track than anything else in the catalog, and almost nobody runs them.

Public procurement filings tell you exactly who has budget locked in. The teams that act on them either apply directly or reach the incumbents being challenged.

M&A gets read as a press release. The reality is a restructuring event: a new CFO is incoming, the vendor list is about to get reviewed, the incumbents are nervous, and fresh stack decisions get made in the first ninety days.

The highest-conviction trigger we have is two signals stacking on the same account in the same week:

1. A reposted job plus a closed round. 
2. A tender filing plus an M&A inside the same vertical.

Those accounts go straight to the top of the list.

Most outbound fails for one reason: it is aimed at people who are not ready to buy yet.

In a crowded market you cannot out-shout that. Sending more just makes you part of the noise people already trained themselves to ignore.

What still gets a reply is timing. 

Reach someone in the short window where they are actively trying to fix the problem you solve, and the same message that dies on a cold list gets answered.

And people tell you when they are in that window. They say it in the open, before they ever go looking for a vendor. 

Someone posts, "anyone know a good tool for X?" A company opens a role to own the exact problem you solve. 

Right there, they raised their hand. 

Your job is to be watching when it happens, and to reach out about that specific thing rather than your usual pitch.

So pick the few signals that mean someone in your market just entered the buying window. Watch for them daily, not once a quarter. When one fires, respond within hours while it is still warm, with one real message that shows you actually noticed. Then let a sequence handle the follow-up.

That is the stack we built at @Sortlist to run this end to end. 

It catches the signal the day it happens, checks it against ten years of our matching data to cut the noise, and runs the sequence through Overloop with Claude writing each message, so you reach people the day they are ready instead of three weeks late.

In a market this crowded, the reply goes to whoever gets there first with something that fits the moment.

A no-show is a qualified lead who just hit a scheduling conflict.

The real problem is manual follow-up: it doesn't work. We forget, we hesitate, we do it once and stop.

So at @Sortlist we set this up as a sequence in Overloop AI, in a few clicks, so it runs on its own instead of depending on anyone to remember. Four touches, two channels:

> 1 hour after the miss (email) 

Short, no blame. "Looks like something slipped into your calendar. Here's a link to rebook in 2 clicks."

Next day (LinkedIn) Same tone but you're reaching them in a different channel. 

"Putting the link here too, just in case."

> Day 3 (email) 

No ask. One insight tied to their industry. You stay top of mind without being heavy.

> Day 7 (email) 

Last call. "If the timing's off now, tell me. Otherwise let's lock it in."

The sequence takes the emotion out of it. It just runs.
We get about 30% of our no-shows back this way.

Stop treating no-shows as losses. They're qualified leads with a calendar problem.

Your highest-intent buyers never fill out a form.

But they all do the same things before they buy: 

hit pricing three times in a week, each visit shorter than the last, rage-click a CTA that loads too slow, and keep checking your integrations page against the competitor they're trying to leave.

On an average, about 9 of every 100 anonymous visitors are buyers. The other 91 are noise (bots, competitor analysts, your own team between meetings), and standard analytics rolls all 100 into one number, so you never see the 9.

Those 9 are the easiest deals you will ever close. They have already decided to buy, and the only thing in their way is friction on your own site. And nobody can sell you this signal. Job changes, funding rounds, competitor likes are public, and every vendor pulls the same feed the same morning. Your traffic sits on your servers, where only you can see it.

Identifying these visitors is not hard. 

Two queries against your own analytics do most of the work: 

Per anonymous visitor, count repeat visits to pricing in a week, and re-tag every form error and abandoned demo to the visitor, not the page. 

The harder part is matching that visitor to a real company or person, which any visitor-ID tool will do, ours or anyone else's.

Then time the outreach to the pattern, but never mention the visit. "I saw you hit our pricing page three times" gets you reported as a creep. Open with something they did in public, a post they commented on, and let the visit set only the timing.

Every "no" in your outbound is telling you something, and almost everyone throws it away.

Most of us log the outcome and move on. Won, lost, no reply. Fine for a dashboard, useless for the next email.

The reason is where the signal hides.

"No" on its own is noise. 
"No, wrong quarter" is a timing trigger. 
"No, already using a competitor" is a displacement play for later. 
"No, not the buyer" is a contact-data fix.

Same word but a different meaning each time.

So capture the reason behind every reply. One line, somewhere you already look: a sheet, your CRM, a notes doc.

Then it pays you back. 

Next time you work the list, the accounts whose moment has finally come surface on their own, instead of you starting cold every quarter.

Not every buying signal deserves a human.

Most teams treat every signal the same. A content download and a week of pricing-page visits land in the same queue, a rep works them in whatever order, and the hot accounts go cold while someone writes a careful note to a tire-kicker.

The solution is a routing rule. Score each account by readiness, then send it to the right responder.

Human, today: the pricing page hit repeatedly this week, a competitor or review-site comparison, or an inbound reply. High intent and time-sensitive. A person sends a short, specific note.

Agent: a role opened that maps to a pain you solve, or a tech or integration change. Real but early. An agent runs a value-first touch, no pitch.

Nurture: a single download or a newsletter open. Curiosity, not intent. It goes on an educational drip until something stronger shows up.

Ignore: no fit, or every signal is stale. Suppress it so it stops eating attention.

A couple of rules keep it honest. When signals conflict, route to the higher tier and say why. And never act on a signal that isn't actually there.

That's the whole rubric. Here's a simple prompt to help you get started (check the next tweet):

Prompt to paste in Claude Code:

You are my signal router.
Input: every buying signal we have for one account (source, recency, intensity).

Score the account's readiness, then route it:
- human: high readiness and time-sensitive (pricing revisits, competitor comparison, an inbound reply)
- agent: real but early (a role you map to a pain, a tech change, content engagement)
- nurture: curiosity only (a single download, a newsletter open)
- ignore: no ICP fit, or every signal is stale

Return only: route, a one-line reason, the first move, and the single best opening angle pulled from the strongest signal.
If signals conflict, route to the higher tier and say why.
Never invent a signal that isn't in the input.

Most AI outbound is one agent told to do the whole job. 

Find the companies, write the emails, send them, chase the follow-ups. All in one prompt.

It demos great. Then week two hits, replies dry up, and you can't tell which part broke. 

So you rip the whole thing out and blame the model.

I split mine into six small Claude Code skills instead. One file each, one job each. When something stops working, I know exactly which file to open.

One watches for the accounts that actually moved this week. A new round, a job change, a competitor suddenly getting attention. 

The next drops the ones that don't matter. 

One writes, but only when there's a real reason to. 

One stays silent on everyone else, which most weeks is the whole job.

The send runs on Overloop, the engine we already run at @Sortlist. 

The last one reads what comes back and feeds it forward, so next week's list is a little smarter than the last.

Most people run outbound as one big task, then wonder why it breaks.

It breaks because one task hides a chain of separate jobs, and the moment any one of them is weak the whole thing leaks. You can't fix what you can't see.

So I split mine into steps and gave each one its own Claude skill:

> detect: find the accounts showing intent this week.
> resolve: turn an anonymous signal into a named company.
> research: build a one-page brief before anyone reaches out.
> score: decide who gets a human, an agent, or nothing.
> draft: open on the signal, not a template.
> sequence: schedule the follow-ups across channels.
> recover: re-open the no-shows and the threads that went quiet.
> log: record why each reply happened, so the next run is smarter.

Each one is a small, readable .md file. I can open any step, see what it does, and fix it without touching the rest. A folder I paste, not a team I manage.

Here's the full stack, one skill per reply. Copy what you need:

Skill 7: recover.md (copy paste into your Claude Code)

You are my recovery agent.

Input: an export of opportunities (last touch, last reply, stage, meeting status).

Classify each: no_show, ghosted_after_reply, dormant, active.

For each non-active record, pick the play:
- no_show: warm reschedule, assume a conflict, offer specific times
- ghosted: reference their last message, lower the ask
- dormant: pattern-break on what changed on their side

Draft each in my voice. No guilt, no "just following up". 

Output a table: record, play, channel, message, send-after date.

Skill 6: sequence.md (copy paste into your Claude Code)

You are my sequencer.

Input: the opener and the channels I allow (email, LinkedIn).

Build a multi-touch sequence across channels. Each touch adds one new angle and never repeats the last:
- the opener
- a proof point
- a different entry (a peer, a resource)
- a clean breakup

Return each touch, its channel, and the wait before it. Keep every message short.

Skill 8: log.md (copy paste into your Claude Code)

After every reply, append one row your agent can read back (a sheet, Airtable, or a replies.jsonl):

{
account: ""
signal_that_started_it: ""
outcome: won | lost | no_reply | not_now
reason: "" // the real why, not just "no"
route_back_when: "" // the trigger that makes them ready again
next_check: "" // a date
}

Log the reason, not just the reply. detect.md reads this on the next run and re-surfaces accounts whose route_back_when has fired. That's the loop.

Everyone obsesses over their cold email copy. Almost nobody obsesses over when it lands.

Timing beats copy, and it is not close. The sharpest email you can write still loses to an average one that shows up the week someone started looking.

Bought lead lists are the most overrated asset in B2B. The data is fine the day you buy it. It goes stale the moment after, and you keep working it like it is still live.

Think about what a list actually is. 

A name, a title, a company, and a timestamp from whenever someone scraped it. It tells you who a person was on the day they got added, and nothing about what is happening in their market today.

And this week is what matters. 

Someone who looked perfect six months ago might have just signed with your competitor. 

Someone who ghosted you last quarter might have raised a round on Tuesday and is buying everything in sight. 

The list knows none of it. It cannot. It is a photo of a moment that already passed.

Watch how the buy side of a market behaves and you notice what a list cannot show. 

Demand never sits still. 

Companies start looking for a vendor every day, well before they land on anyone's radar. That motion is the only real signal, and a bought list has none of it.

So with a list you do the only thing it lets you do. You blast everyone and hope. You send 1,000 emails to reach the 20 people who happen to be ready, and you burn the other 980 to get there.

Signal-based outbound runs the other way. 

You start from the motion. 

Someone opens a role they only open right before they buy. Someone drops the tool you replace. Someone closes a round. 

That is the moment a stranger becomes worth a message.

Then the real work starts, and the work is restraint more than anything else. Score the why-now, pick the handful that matter, let the rest be. Only then does someone get an email, written off the real trigger. 

TL;DR: A bought lead list just tells you who people were. The market tells you who is ready now. Build from the second one.

Switching your follow-ups from dates to signals is the biggest hack in outbound right now.

Day 3, day 7, day 11 is a schedule you invented. Nothing happened at the account between those dates, so email two says what email one said with a "just bumping this" on top. Everyone reads that for what it is.

So what do you do? Just like you time outbound with signals, do the same thing for replies. Follow-up with them when you identify a buying signal on their end. 

The flow:

1. Pick the triggers that mean something in your market. A role opening on the team you sell into, a round closing, a competitor tool dropping off their stack, a new person in the seat that owns the budget.

2. Park every no-reply account on a watch list instead of a drip. Kill the scheduled sends.

3. When a trigger fires, that account comes off the watch list and gets one email written off the trigger.

4. Open on the change, never on the history. "Circling back on my last email" throws away the reason you are sending at all.

Do this and you end up with a second first touch. 

But there's an obvious trade-off here...accounts that never move never hear from you again. Those were the ones that were going to ignore you anyway.

New LinkedIn connections are one of the most underrated buying signals in B2B.

When someone at a target account connects with your competitor's AE, then their solutions engineer a week later, that account is in a live evaluation. Nobody connects with salespeople for fun. 

And it works in both directions. 

Your prospects' new connections tell you when a known account starts buying. Whereas a competitor rep's new connections are a feed of in-market accounts you did not know existed.

Here is how to capture this signal (using Claude Code) start to finish:

1. Write two watchlists into plain text files. 

File one: the sales team at your top two competitors. AE, SDR, solutions engineer, head of sales. 10 to 15 profiles. 

File two: the buying-committee people at your top 20 target accounts. That is the whole setup.

2. Give Claude Code the Monday sweep. 

It opens each profile's public activity and logs who reacted and commented, on both lists. 

The names that keep turning up around the reps are accounts in evaluation, including accounts you have never touched.

3. Have it keep one record per account: 

Person, date, what they touched. 

It appends every run, dedupes against what it already saw, and drops the job seekers, fans, and vendors on title alone.

4. One rule in the config: 

Two sightings in 30 days = hot. Those accounts get flagged to the top, above every scored lead you have.

5. For every flagged account, it drafts the opener. 

On the problem their evaluation is trying to solve, never on what it saw. "Noticed you know their AE" is creepy. Every message stays a draft until you approve it, so you've the final word on things. 

6. No reply? The account stays on the watchlist and the next sign of intent restarts the clock. 

Connections themselves are mostly invisible on LinkedIn... but  engagement is public, and the same buyers do both, which is why the sweep works at all. 

Two text files and a cron line. Works embarrassingly well.

Say you catch four funding rounds one quarter and none of them convert. Bad timing, and two were bridge rounds.

So the system does the sensible thing and lowers the weight on funding.

Now accounts that just raised stop making your list. You stop reaching them, so none of them book anything, because nobody asked. Next quarter funding looks worse still, and the weight drops again.

The signals that die this way are always the rare ones.

Post reactions fire constantly, so they carry enough volume to climb back out. A funding round or a new VP landing in the budget seat shows up a handful of times a quarter. Two bad ones bury the signal that was probably worth the most.

Six months on, nobody can tell you why funding accounts stopped showing up.

Give every signal a minimum it can never fall below. Even the losing ones keep pushing a few accounts through each week. That's the part I would not build one of these without.

So before you let it run on its own: can a signal that stopped working ever come back?

If it cannot, it will keep narrowing until it only watches whatever happens most often. And what happens most often is rarely what buys.

Buyers write differently when no seller is in the room.

They explain:

- what disappointed them
- what took too long

Emailing the reviewer directly is creepy.

Use the reviews as research.

1. Pick one competitor or product category.

2. Pull recent reviews from G2 or Capterra.

Focus on detailed reviews because a one-line complaint gives you very little to work with.

3. Paste the reviews into Claude with this prompt:

“Group the exact phrases by pain, desired result, objection, switching trigger and decision risk. Keep the buyer’s words. Do not paraphrase.”

4. Remove the one-off complaints.

Keep the phrases that appear across different companies and reviewers.

5. Map each recurring pain to the person who usually owns it.

onboarding problem → operations
reporting problem → marketing leadership
migration problem → IT

6. Wait for separate evidence from a company you actually want to contact.

- website visit
- job post
- competitor mention
- technology change

7. Use the recurring pain in the email.

Better:

Approval to hire doesn't tell you whether there's money for your product.

Here's everything I think you should know if you're building GTM bots with AI.

I've built them on 8 different AI setups so far this year: Claude, GLM, Codex, Kimi, GPT-6 Astra, Grok, Fable and Jev.

Before you build (1-5)

1. Run ten accounts yourself first, fifteen minutes each. Every field you find missing becomes the spec.
2. Give the bot your offer and your ICP side by side before it researches anyone. Hand it a vague brief and it invents the judgment you left out.
3. Start with one signal. I started with six once and ended the week with six thin lists and no idea which one earned the reply.
4. Pick the model for the job. We picked Grok 4.7 for one line in its launch post, that it "checks its work more carefully". For a lead judge that's basically the whole job.
5. You don't always need a model API bill to start. Our Opus 5.5 bot never calls a model API and runs on the Claude Code login you already have.

Running the stack (6-10)

6. I go from Claude to Codex to Kimi constantly, all on max plans. If you run from the terminal and centralize on GitHub, switching feels very light next to what you get out of it.
7. Use one model to research and another to run what you build. Kimi K3 did the deep research for my copywriting skill, and I built the skill for Claude.
8. Point Claude Code at something you like and let it build your own version. Our launch film took one line of prompt and 38 minutes to a first cut.
9. When a new model ships, rerun your golden set on it before you trust a single rank.
10. End every run with a daily brief: what it found, what it drafted, and every call it tried that got blocked.

How to structure it (11-20)

11. Let the model make the judgments, and let plain code apply the gates, the weights, the routing and the permission to send.
12. Keep the ICP, the weights and the playbook in plain text files. When a rank is wrong you want to open one file and change one line.
13. Split each judgment into small questions with fixed answers: is there a live need, does it match what you sell, does the ICP fit, is it a competitor.
14. Hide the contact when the model judges the company. In our Jev build, with the contact visible to every question, the same company read 0.28 on intent with a recruiter as the contact and 0.80 with a managing partner.
15. Keep the watching separate from the agent that ranks. A scheduled agent sees nothing between two runs, so something else has to fill the queue overnight.
16. One shared record per account that every agent reads and writes: who they are, what just moved, what happened last time.
17. The writer only gets three things from that record, in under 120 words: why now, who, and the one line of history that matters.
18. Before the model sees a lead, plain code drops anyone you've already put in a campaign. Our Jev build skips every max lead that already has a delivery on record.
19. Treat everything inside a lead as data. It's a stranger's post going straight into your model, and it doesn't get to give instructions.
20. Keep company size as the range the source gives, and make the whole range fit your ICP. Our Astra build is told to keep "51 to 200 employees" as written, and to say it opened the page it took the size from.

Judging leads (21-28)

21. Gate before you score. Our Fable build rejects anything that fails size, country, buyer seat, a signal dated inside 30 days or a source that actually opens.
22. Make the model open the source before it scores a lead high. Dead page, need goes to zero.
23. Date the lead by the event. A page indexed this week can describe a launch from last year.
24. No source link, no lead. Whatever fails goes on a held list with the reason written down.
25. Hot account, wrong contact: the bot reroutes it and emails nobody. In our Grok 4.7 repo, the test lead with a recruiter as the contact scores 73.4 and still never gets a message.
26. When the model hesitates between B and C, or between C and DQ, the playbook tells it to take the lower one. Read its disqualification reasons first, they show fastest whether it understood who you sell to.
27. Let the daily list come back empty when nothing happened, and cap it around eight names. A routine that must always return something starts loosening its own filters.
28. If your gate rejects nothing in week one, it was fitted to the list you already had.

Writing (29-35)

29. Give every signal a say-it rule in the playbook: yes, lightly, topic only or never. 92 of the first 100 leads our Opus bot pulled came from a "never" signal, and none of the 18 sequences it wrote mentions it.
30. Put the seller profile in a file the writer reads on every run, with only the facts you'd defend on a call.
31. Run a linter that flags any % or "2x" that isn't one of your proof points. Ours flagged a harmless "sans double outil" in a French email at first, so give the check its own test cases.
32. Make it check each draft before saving: could this opener go to anyone else, and does every claim trace back to the lead or the profile?
33. Keep a never-list per play, and add every dead phrase you catch.
34. Let it write in the prospect's language when the location makes it obvious. Our first Opus run came back in French, German and English.
35. When a reply asks for something that isn't in your facts, the draft should promise the figures and flag the gap. Answering one simulated test reply, ours did that and still slipped in "depends on seats and volume", which isn't in our profile. Every reply draft waits for a human to send it.

Safety (36-43)

36. Default to locked. Going live should be a flag you flip on purpose.
37. Every campaign the bot creates starts switched off. In our Opus test run that was 18 campaigns and zero people enrolled.
38. Keep approving, launching and ICP changes out of the scheduled run.
39. Log every write the bot attempts, allowed or blocked. We tried to break the lock three times on our live workspace: twice with a safety script, once by launching an approved campaign while send mode was locked. The guard blocked 7 calls and the daily brief listed every one.
40. Tag everything the bot creates with one name prefix, so you can list it and delete it in one go.
41. Put a daily cap on anything that costs money or creates something.
42. Make the bot re-check for replies, bounces and opt-outs right before it enrolls anyone. A human review sits between building a campaign and launching it, and people can reply or opt out in between.
43. Read at least 20 sequences in review before you flip send mode to live.

Testing and learning (44-50)

44. Build a small golden set with the traps in it: a recruiter at a hot account, a competitor, a company stacking press releases. On our Jev starter set the ranker gets 10 of 10, the offline baseline gets 7.
45. Write tests for the routing too. Someone who already replied should never land in a new sequence, whatever the model thinks.
46. Make the reason a required field in the outcome log. A bare "no reply" teaches the next run almost nothing.
47. Leave the weights alone until each bucket has 30 real contacts. After its first run our Opus bot called its 15 simulated outcomes "not evidence". Fair.
48. Cap how far a weight can move in a day, and give every signal a floor so the rare ones don't get buried.
49. Route a few leads below your line to a one-touch lane. If the bot only ever contacts the top, you never find out the line is in the wrong place.
50. Change one thing per round. Our Codex build proposes one change at a time as a pull request, and a human merges it.

Most bad AI outbound comes from one thing: the model can't see what you know.

I turned Claude into a prospecting analyst with five prompts (in the article below). Here's what we learned to tell it, so the emails come out right.

If it makes things up:

1. Give it the actual page, the job post, the funding announcement. Don't let it work from a search snippet. That's where the congratulations email for a round nobody raised comes from.

2. Ask it to put the source next to every fact. If it can't point to one, delete the fact.

3. Keep two dates on every fact: when it happened, and when you found it. A page you found this morning can be about last spring.

The job post in the article had no date at all, so part of the hold was checking the role was still open.

4. Tell it what it's not allowed to guess. Ours can't guess budget, urgency or whether someone is ready to buy from a single event. A funding round that says nothing about sales is a weak reason to pitch sales.

If every email could go to anyone

5. Give it the reason you'd matter to them this week. Twenty cold emails a day can name the city I posted from. Not one of them knows if I have a problem.

6. Be exact. Which role they reposted, how much they raised, what the tender actually says. "They fit our ICP" gives it nothing to write with.

7. A test I like: cut the line about what you found and read the email again. If it still sounds like a decent email, send it. If it falls apart, that one line was doing all the work.

8. Keep a short list of things it may never write, next to the instructions. A model can follow every tone instruction and still write the exact email buyers delete on sight.

Ours started as four lines: no buzzwords, no em dashes, no fake urgency or "circling back", no "Hi {{firstName}}". It's longer now, and it does more than the instructions do.

If it pitches the wrong person

9. The person in the news isn't always the person who buys. A company posts its first SDR role. The person they hire is nobody to you.

Whoever runs the sales team is probably who you want, and even that stays a guess until someone has checked. Never let it make up a name.

10. Ask it to make the case against the lead in the same answer. A company hiring its first outbound rep looks like the perfect lead for outbound consulting.

It's also a company that just decided to build it in-house. My call on that one was hold.

If it opens with what it found

11. "Saw you raised your Series B" tells them a tool found it. Counting their pricing-page visits out loud is worse. What you found sets the timing and the topic. The first line is about something they did in public.

If it says yes to everyone

12. Let it say "not yet". Ours says hold when the fit looks right but something still needs checking, and nothing goes out until a person has checked it. A reason to stop is a useful answer.

13. Keep the first email small. 70 words at most: one thing you can back up, one thing you can actually send, one simple question. If what you're sending is a blank template, call it a template.

If it never gets better

14. Log the reason behind every no, in one line. "Wrong quarter" is a date to come back. "Already with a competitor" is a different angle later. "Not the buyer" is a contact to fix. Same word, three different next moves.

15. When the answer is wrong, change what it can see before you rewrite the instruction. Anthropic's own prompting video gets Claude from a wrong insurance ruling to the right one without really touching the instruction. Most bad answers are missing a fact.

You can book more meetings from outbound all while contacting fewer people.

Earlier this year, we ran outbound on 142 leads that had all shown a buying signal. 12% of them replied, where cold usually sits around 2 to 3%, and we booked 19 meetings in two weeks.

Same on the phone. A recent cold call session on a warm intent list got me an 80% connection rate (I dial everyone twice) and 15% meetings booked.

So what changed? Mostly who we contact, and when. Here are 20 tips to help you do the same with signal-based outbound:

Your ICP first
1. Check it against the deals you actually closed. I did this on our HubSpot and mine was skipping 1-10 employee companies... 178 of my won deals were exactly those.
2. When I split my 500 won deals by industry, size and country, they came out as 3 segments. I'd give each one its own ICP.
3. One campaign per ICP too, or your first line ends up generic for everybody.
4. Before you approve a lead, check it's not already in your CRM. You really don't want to cold pitch someone who's already a customer.

Who goes on the list
5. A job posted for the second time is worth a look. Usually it means they're struggling to fill it.
6. Almost nobody watches public tenders, they're a pain to track. But the budget is there, and the person to contact is at the public body that published it.
7. Look for two different signals on the same account. Someone engaging with your competitor AND a new role opening on that team, that's interesting. Two likes, not so much.
8. A new VP or C-level arriving is the strongest one we've seen. They usually take a fresh look at their vendors in the first 90 days.
9. For every person on the list, write one line on why this week. If you can't, they probably shouldn't be there yet.

Calling
10. Only look up mobile numbers for the people you'll call this week. It's the most expensive thing to enrich, so I leave it for last.
11. Act quickly on a signal. After a funding round I'd say about two weeks, a reorg gives you a bit longer, maybe a month.
12. If an account with real potential opens your emails a few times, I call.

Website visitors
13. Use a visit for timing only. What you say should come from something they did in public, like a post they commented on.
14. And please never mention the visit, it just reads as creepy.
15. Before you act on one, double check you matched the right company and that the page they read has something to do with what you sell.

After that
16. When leads go into your sequencer, keep the signal attached, so whoever writes the email knows why you're reaching out now. Ours go to Overloop AI.
17. Read the source behind each signal before approving, sometimes it says something else than what you expected.
18. Auto-accept on new leads is fine once the fit scores mostly look right to you. Older leads stay manual anyway.
19. When deals close, go back and check which signals they came from, and watch more of those.
20. No CRM connected? Take your last ten wins and write down what was going on at each account in the month before you first spoke.

New VP + fresh round at the same company = the best buying signal you can target for B2B

Of the several buying signals we track, no pair converts better. Several times our cold baseline.

So the rule is simple:

VP in the seat < 90 days + round announced < 2 weeks ago = drop everything else.

How to find such leads (with https://t.co/shO8OijHTg):

1. Switch on two watches: job changes for the titles you sell to, and funding rounds.
2. Every day, https://t.co/shO8OijHTg gives you a fresh shortlist, with the reason and the evidence behind each lead.
3. Put any company that shows up in both at the top.
4. Open the profile. Start date under 90 days, and they own the budget.
5. max drafts the first email. You edit it, approve it, and push the lead to Overloop AI.

On that email, leave the round and the new role out of it. Most folks who reach out would open with something basic like "congrats" that same week. Don't do that. Don't mention any of the signals you've tracked.

Write about what they now have to deliver with the money, and the one piece of it you can take off their plate.
